articles.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
keyFacts: Italian regulators fined Meta €805m for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta failed to properly inform about 20 million users about the gallery access feature.
The regulator gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
body: - Published
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.headline: So, What Will Democrats Do Next Year? They’re Working On That.
keyFacts: Democrats won Congress on an affordability message and are now determining how to prioritize their agenda under President Donald Trump.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, urging Democrats to leverage upcoming government funding deadlines.
Democrats generally agree on reversing tariffs and healthcare cuts, though passing laws will require cooperation or vetoes from Trump.
body: WASHINGTON — Democrats won Congress in a landslide on an “affordability” message responding to voter frustration with persistently high prices under President Donald Trump. Now they have to figure out how to deliver on it — even with Trump still in office.

Their to-do list is long. But figuring out what to prioritize, how far to push for it and what they can actually get with Trump still in the White House won’t be an easy task, and could split the party’s post-election unity.

“We need to end the war of choice in Iran,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters Thursday. “We need to stop the Trump tariffs. We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We need to reverse the [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program] cuts. We need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) sketched out a similar agenda in a meeting with his colleagues this week; they talked through their plan for the first 100 days of the next Congress.

But there’s a chance — although still a small one — that Schumer won’t be the party’s leader come January. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is challenging Schumer for the majority leader job next year, and is already signaling a tactical break with Schumer.

Van Hollen wants to use a coming expiration of government funding, set for Dec. 11, to demand that Trump end his war in Iran. The move would amount to a replay of Democrats’ gambit in the fall of 2025, when they shut down the government to demand Trump extend health care subsidies. While the subsidies weren’t extended, the party showed fight to its base and Trump’s callous actions during the shutdown — threatening to end food aid, tearing down the East Wing of the White House — damaged his approval rating.
“We should do it now. We shouldn’t say we’re going to wait till January when we have the power to do it on Dec. 11,” Van Hollen said this week on MS NOW.

The top Democratic appropriators — the people who write government funding bills — aren’t on board yet, but they’ve said they’re considering it. A shutdown that extended into the new year could overshadow other parts of the affordability agenda.

Democrats still have major points of agreement, after all. They seem set on following through on campaign promises to undo the SNAP and Medicaid cuts Republicans enacted last year and roll back some of his high-end tax cuts, though it’s unclear whether they will pass individual bills for each item or separate ones. More bills, the thinking goes, would make it more politically damaging for Trump to use his veto pen, as he’s promised to do.

Interviews with a dozen House and Senate Democrats this week also found wide agreement on undoing Trump’s tariffs, which have increased prices for consumer goods, and passing an ethics bill that would ban stock trading not just for members of Congress, but also for the executive branch and for the courts.

Getting any of this into law will almost certainly require cooperation from Trump, which has some Democrats reviving an old dream of Trump agreeing to progressive ideas in hopes of salvaging political wins.

“If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality,” Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) said on Thursday at the Majority Democrats conference in Denver. “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history.”

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) tried pitching “Medicare For All” to Trump on social media, posting an image of gold “TrumpCare” cards that would let the president claim credit for a policy most famously promoted by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).
“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote.

It’s not just newcomers fantasizing about a surprise bipartisan turn from Trump, who occasionally negotiated with Democrats in his first term but has largely eschewed such meetings since returning to office.

“There might be the opportunity to be able to do something on immigration, including the Dream Act,” Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), who has served in the Senate since 2009, told HuffPost, describing a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. “It’s a very exciting prospect.”
Even Jeffries has recently said immigration “needs to be fixed in a bipartisan way.”

Trump said in 2018 that he would support an immigration deal with a pathway to citizenship, then rejected the idea almost as soon as a bipartisan group of senators presented it to him, partly because of the influence of Stephen Miller, the virulently anti-immigration aide who is now his chief of staff.
“Trump did a 180 from what he promised,” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) told HuffPost.
Still, some Democrats think it’s important to at least appear to try to be bipartisan.

“I think we first find places where we think we can actually do good for the American public, and maybe that means that we potentially will be working with Donald Trump on bills that could bring down cost of living, increase wages, health care,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) told HuffPost. “If we get that going, that’s great. If not, then we start talking about what messaging looks like and messaging bills and setting up for later.”

The messaging scenario seems more likely. Democrats will pass bills that Trump vetoes. Even to do that, however, Democrats will have to figure out what they want. A lot of Democrats have talked about raising the federal minimum wage for the first time since 2009, for instance, but the party hasn’t figured out how high they want to raise it. Jeffries declined to say when asked on Thursday.
“That’s a great question, and it’s one of the things that we’re working out between the House and the Senate,” he said.

articles.headline: Casualties: Unknown Is A Brutal 97%-Rated Survival Game That Will Make You Realize Your Mortality, And At A Cheap Price, Too
keyFacts: Casualties: Unknown is a brutal survival game on Steam that received a 97% rating from nearly 2,000 reviews.
Players control an Experiment on an alien planet, navigating a fully simulated injury and cardiovascular system across eleven depths.
The indie game is available for a launch-day discount price of $17.24 at Fanatical.
body: There’s no light. The shuttle that brought me into the depths is fitted with just a shower, and the darkness swallows everything around me. Each step is as painful as the last, like walking barefoot on LEGO bricks, as I narrowly miss traps. Corpses are frozen as I head further down, a reminder of who came before and likely what I’ll end up as. I crack the glass of a small base, crawling through to gain access, shrapnel filling my foot as I sneak through. Infection rises, but with no medicine, it spreads. It gets worse. It gets worse. I die.

That was my first run of Casualties: Unknown . I’ve played a lot of survival games, but few are as brutal, as dark, and as thrilling as this Steam game, which has earned the ‘Overwhelmingly Positive’ badge of approval from almost 2,000 reviews, giving it a 97% rating and making it an indie gem. It’s easy to look at its various mechanics and think it sounds challenging, masochistic, and downright terrifying, and those are all accurate. It’s also a game about hope and getting through the hardest times, pushing yourself to become stronger and better.

Let me explain: Casualties sees you play as an ‘Experiment’, the affectionate name given to creatures spliced with human and animal DNA. On an alien planet, your job is to push further into the depths, scavenging alien flora and fauna to craft resources and eventually getting deeper and deeper. However, what makes Casualties so hard is that it has a fully simulated injury and cardiovascular system; one wrong move could leave you dealing with an open wound and nothing to patch it up with.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Sd7HIk41Us

Every run is as customizable as you’d like. You could make it ridiculously easy, albeit still with some challenge, or you could make it a dreadful experience—it’s entirely up to you. Death is practically inevitable, especially when you’re starting out, but each step you take in subsequent runs builds your knowledge, and eventually, you may even make it to the second layer. There are 11, by the way.

It’s easily one of the best indie games I’ve played, offering a blend of an unforgiving world with a dash of hopeful optimism. And despite just launching, you can grab Casualties: Unknown for just $17.24 / £14.24 at Fanatical . That’s a brilliant launch-day discount, and it easily makes it worth playing, whether it’s out of morbid curiosity or the hope that you’ll eventually beat it.
Good luck, either way.

articles.headline: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
keyFacts: Chilean President José Antonio Kast faces a 24% approval rating due to rising fuel costs, controversial prisoner sentence reductions, and widespread public protests.
Truckers recently blockaded major highways over fuel prices, prompting the government to submit a bill to Congress to reverse planned fuel price increases.
Protests are expected to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living while pursuing budget cuts.
body: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

articles.headline: I Let My Apple Watch Eavesdrop on My Conversations for 2 Weeks
keyFacts: Apple Watch models introduced Audio Intelligence, an optional feature featuring Siri Recap and Live Rewind to record and summarize daily conversations.
The CNET reviewer found Siri Recap useful for structured work meetings, but inaccurate and prone to mixing up unrelated daily conversations.
Apple stated the features will be released publicly later this year.
body: We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.
Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.
It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.
The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.
Live Rewind: Late to the trigger
Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.
Siri Recap: Good at meetings, bad at life

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.
One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.
Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)
Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.
Siri’s version:
- Details about medical condition
- Entire case of apple cider ruined after repeated warnings to stop shaking
- No more apple cider will be brought into the house
- Any remaining stickiness on the floor results in no iPad on the plane
It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).
A case for manually enabling Siri Recap during meetings

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.
But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.
If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

articles.headline: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
keyFacts: US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino frequently urged fans and players to believe the team could win the World Cup.
Pochettino faced criticism for persistent rumors linking him to English clubs before he accepted the Manchester United job.
Pochettino stated that his lasting impact on the program was built on relationships and shared values rather than on-field victories.
body: It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.
“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”

It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”
Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

articles.headline: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
keyFacts: Experts argue that preventing campus sexual assault requires comprehensive sex education starting in kindergarten rather than relying solely on punishment and enforcement.
Comprehensive sex education teaches students boundary setting, communication, and mutual desire, which studies suggest lowers the risk of later sexual assault.
Despite bipartisan public support, comprehensive sex education mandates frequently face political opposition and legislative roadblocks in states and at the federal level.
body: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images

In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate.

Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions. Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process. But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025.

It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment. Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way. There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education.

Yes, you read that right: sex ed. But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people. This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states , takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.

An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards . Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.

Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough. Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.

The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand. I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision. Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States. In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives. The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.

The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum. In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty. Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues. They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse. My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business. What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place.

Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens , which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.
“Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health

Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them. In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.)

While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late. By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.”

The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified.

Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.

Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships. Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited. A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college. Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.

This makes intuitive sense. If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens. If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.

Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”

But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs , in states that consider adopting it. Since 2017 , New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12. Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee. At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior.

Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions. They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one. Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it. Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.
If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus. Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

articles.headline: Ubisoft is reportedly making a new Rainbow Six Vegas game, nearly two decades after Vegas 2
keyFacts: Ubisoft Montreal is reportedly developing a new Rainbow Six Vegas game under the codename Spades, according to Insider Gaming.
Insider Gaming sources stated that the project is in early development and is likely to be a new sequel rather than a remake.
Insider Gaming reported that it will be several years before Ubisoft officially announces the new game.
body: Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

According to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades. It’s one of three new projects reportedly in production at the studio, and sources suggest a second of those is also set in the Rainbow Six universe. Eurogamer hasn’t been able to verify the report.

It’s not yet clear what form the new game will take, but Insider Gaming’s sources said it's "likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake" of an existing game. Insider Gaming expects it will be several years before Ubisoft officially announces a new Vegas game.

Rainbow Six Vegas launched in 2006, followed by Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008. Since then, the series has centred on 2015's Rainbow Six Siege, and in August, Ubisoft announced Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player, turn-based spin-off from Ubisoft Paris due in 2027.
Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

Last week, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games: one set in ancient Rome, and a mobile spin-off set in Jerusalem. The leak came less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

articles.headline: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
keyFacts: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope discovered water and carbon dioxide ice in the debris disk surrounding the young star Beta Pictoris.
Researchers reported that the water ice is glassy and mixed with carbon dioxide in proportions similar to comets in our own Solar System.
The discovery suggests that ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds could be common around young stars despite earlier search failures.
body: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.
The missing ice

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.

Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

articles.headline: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
keyFacts: Microsoft announced education price increases and service cuts, retiring free student email and collaboration services.
The UK Department for Education expressed disappointment, as institutions face new recurring bills for previously free features.
Rivals stated that affected institutions have time to plan and migrate to alternative software options before changes begin in 2028.
body: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.
As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants .

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.
A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."
A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.
Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.
"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®
